     Celandine. Papaveraceæ.

     "A perennial plant with a sharp, bitter and burning taste, yielding, when pressed, a yellow, corrosive, milky juice ; it grows in hedges and waste places, among stones and rubbish."

     Tincture from the fresh root, or of the whole plant.

     This remedy, famous in antiquity, preserved its repute through the Middle Ages. It was administered in serious complaints, particularly in hepatic derangement, according to the law of signatura, the yellow juice of the plant against the yellow bile and jaundiced look. It was proved by Hahnemann, and later more extensively by O. Buchmann, of Alvensleben (vide Encyclopædia, vol. 3). Its place in the Materia Medica is well defined by numerous clinical reports verifying the provings.

     Most symptoms marked '(In sick :)' are pathogenetic observations by Berridge.

TIME. [38] [Chel.]

Towards evening : repeated chill, dry heat ; cheeks red, head and left eye very hot.

RELATIONS. [48] [Chel.]
Antidoted by : Acon., when the circulation becomes excited ; acids, wine and coffee restrict its action.
It antidotes : Bryon.
Compatible : Arsen., Bryon., Cor. rub. (pertussis), Ipec. (spasm of glottis), Ledum, Sulphur (hepatized lung).
Compare : Acon., Arsen., Baryta, Bellad., Bryon., Calcar., Capsic., Chelerythrin, Chen. ant., Cinchon., Corall. (whooping cough), Gambog. (diarrhœa), Graphit., Ignat., Lycop. (liver ; pneumonia, one foot cold), Mercur. (pneumonia, with liver complications), Nitr. ac., Nux vom., Opium (family relation), Phosphor. (chest, yellow diarrhœa), Podoph. (liver), Pulsat., Rhus tox., Sanguin. (family relation), Selen., Sepia, Silic., Spigel., Sulphur and Viol. od.
